question_text: A patient's temporal bone imaging shows an ossicle marked in the lateral section of the middle ear. Which pharyngeal arch does this structure develop from?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The structure marked is the malleus, one of the auditory ossicles of the middle ear.
  • Malleus develops from Meckel's cartilage of the first pharyngeal (mandibular) arch.
  • The first pharyngeal arch is innervated by the mandibular and maxillary branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).

question_text: Which of the following foramina pierce the sphenoid bone?

explanation:

  • It contributes to the floor of the middle cranial fossa, lateral wall of the skull, and posterolateral wall of the orbit.
  • Three key foramina pierce the greater wing of the sphenoid:
    • Foramen rotundum → transmits the maxillary nerve
    • Foramen ovale → transmits the mandibular nerve
    • Foramen spinosum → transmits the middle meningeal vessels
  • These foramina are critical anatomical landmarks and are involved in neurovascular transmission.

  • Option D - Includes foramen lacerum: Incorrect - the foramen lacerum is located between the sphenoid, temporal, and occipital bones and is not a true opening through the sphenoid bone.

question_text: Which movement is produced by the muscle attached at the marked point?

  • Assisted by suprahyoid muscleswhen the hyoid bone is stabilized.
  • The lateral pterygoid musclehas two heads.
    • The superior head arises from the infratemporal surface and infratemporal crest of the greater wing of the sphenoid bone and inserts into the pterygoid fovea. It is supplied by the nerve to the lateral pterygoid, a branch of the anterior division of the mandibular nerve (CN V₃), with separate branches to each head. Its primary action is to stabilize the articular disc during mandibular closing and to help prevent posterior displacement during clenching.

It is also supplied by the lateral pterygoid nerve of CN V₃. question_text: Which of the following bones develops through intramembranous ossification?
explanation:
Frontal bones undergo intramembranous ossification. Other bones listed have enchondral ossification.

Based on their development, bones can be classified into 3 categories:

  1. Membranous bones (dermal bones) are formed through intramembranous ossification. There is direct bone formation within highly vascular sheets or 'membranes' derived from mesenchymal
    condensations. e.g., bones of the facial skeleton including the frontal, lacrimal, zygomatic, and nasal bones.
  2. Cartilaginous bones are formed by intra-cartilaginous (enchondral) ossification.
    Bone forms by ossification of preformed hyaline cartilage model. This is the main method of bone formation in the body. e.g., bones of limbs, vertebral column, and thoracic cage.
  3. Membranocartilaginous bones ossify from both cartilage and mesenchymal condensation. e.g., clavicle, mandible, occipital bone, temporal bone, sphenoid bone, etc.

question_text: Paralysis of which muscle causes ptosis in Horner's syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ptosis in Horner's syndrome is primarily due to the paralysis of the superior tarsal muscle (also known as Müller's muscle).

  • This muscle is responsible for maintaining the eyelid position and lifting the upper eyelid slightly.
  • In Horner's syndrome, the sympathetic innervation to the superior tarsal muscle is disrupted, resulting in ptosis (drooping of the eyelid).

Explanation for other options:

Orbitalis (Option B): The orbitalis muscle is not involved in ptosis. It helps in closing the eyelids but does not contribute to the sympathetic control of the eyelid.

Orbicularis oculi (Option C): This muscle is responsible for closing the eyelid, but ptosis in Horner's syndrome is caused by a sympathetic defect affecting the superior tarsal muscle, not the orbicularis oculi.

Sphincter pupillae (Option D): The sphincter pupillae muscle is responsible for pupil constriction (miosis) under parasympathetic control, not related to ptosis in Horner's syndrome.

question_text: A student experiences jaw locking during a yawn. Spasm of which muscle, attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint, is most likely responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The lateral pterygoid muscle is the only muscle attached to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ).

It plays a key role in the movement of the TMJ, particularly in opening the mouth and moving the jaw forward (protraction).

Lateral pterygoid:

Attachment: The superior head of the lateral pterygoid inserts into the articular disc and the joint capsule, while the inferior head attaches to the neck of the mandible.

Function: It helps in:

Depressing the mandible (opening the mouth).

Protrusion and lateral movements of the jaw.

Spasmodic contraction: During excessive yawning, prolonged contraction of the lateral pterygoid can pull the articular disc and the mandible forward, potentially leading to jaw locking due to dislocation of the TMJ.

Explanation for other options:

Temporalis (Option B): This muscle primarily elevates and retracts the mandible; it has no attachment to the articular disc.

Medial pterygoid (Option C): Assists in elevation and side-to-side movements of the mandible but is not connected to the articular disc.

Masseter (Option D): A strong elevator of the mandible; also has no attachment to the articular disc.

question_text: All of the following is true about the frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle, EXCEPT:
option_a: Frontal bellies don't have bony attachments
option_b: Frontal bellies supplied by zygomatic branch of facial nerve
option_c: Both the side frontal belies are longer and united with each other medially
option_d: They produce transverse wrinkles on the forehead
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Occipitofrontalis covers the dome of the skull from the highest nuchal lines to the eyebrows. It is a broad, musculo-fibrous layer and consists of four thin, muscular quadrilateral parts, two occipital and two frontal, connected by the epicranial aponeurosis.
  • Occipital bellies:
    • Each occipital part (occipitalis) arises by tendinous fibres from the lateral two-thirds of the highest nuchal line of the occipital bone and the adjacent region of the mastoid part of the temporal bone to extend forward and join the aponeurosis. The gap between the two occipital parts is occupied by an extension of the epicranial aponeurosis.
  • Frontal Bellies:
    • Each frontal part (frontalis) is adherent to the superficial fascia, particularly of the eyebrows. Although frontalis has no bony attachments of its own, its fibres blend with those of adjacent muscles, procerus, corrugator supercilii and orbicularis oculi, and ascend to join the epicranial aponeurosis anterior to the coronal suture (Option A)
  • Nerve Supply:
    • The occipital part of occipitofrontalis is supplied by the posterior auricular branch of the facial nerve.
    • The frontal part is supplied by the temporal branches of the facial nerve
  • Actions:
    • Acting from above, the frontal parts raise the eyebrows and the skin over the root of the nose (e.g. as in expressions of surprise or horror). Acting from below, the frontal parts draw the scalp forwards, throwing the forehead into transverse wrinkles. (Option D)
    • The occipital parts draw the scalp backwards.

Key Takeaway:

The frontal bellies of the occipitofrontalis muscle lack bony attachments, are supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve and play a major role in facial expressions like raising eyebrows and wrinkling the forehead.

question_text: A patient had surgery in the left carotid triangle complained to her physician that she has little sense of touch to the skin over the left side of her neck and difficulty swallowing. The patient's tongue is not affected. The physician suspects that the cervical plexus of nerves to the left side of her patient's neck was harmed during the surgical procedure. Loss of touch sensation to the skin over the anterior triangle would result from injury to which nerve?
explanation:
Transverse cervical nerve. The cervical plexus is situated deep in the upper part of the neck, under cover of the internal jugular vein and the sternocleidomastoid (SCM). Formed by the anterior primary rami of cervical nerves 1-3, it gives rise to superficial branches, which emerge near the middle of the posterior border of the SCM.

The branches are :

  1. The lesser occipital nerve, which hooks around the accessory nerve and ascends to the auricle
  2. The great auricular nerve which ascends superficial to the SCM and toward the parotid region
  3. The transverse cervical nerve, which crosses the SCM into the anterior neck; and
  4. The supraclavicular nerves, which descend as three nerves that cross the clavicle and supply the skin over the shoulder.

question_text: At which anatomical level is the common carotid artery pulse palpated?
explanation:
Explanation:

The common carotid artery ascends within the carotid sheath in the neck and bifurcates at the level of the superior border of the thyroid cartilage.

  • Clinically, the pulse of the common carotid artery is palpated at the level of the cricoid cartilage, within the carotid triangle.
  • The carotid triangle is a clinically significant landmark for vascular assessment, surgical access, and nerve identification.

Carotid triangle:

Explanation of Other Options:

Laryngeal prominence(Option B):

  • The laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple) corresponds to the thyroid cartilage of the larynx, typically at the C4 vertebral level.
  • The common carotid artery lies posterolateral to the thyroid cartilage, so while it is close, the pulse is more reliably felt at the cricoid cartilage (C6 level) in the carotid triangle.
  • Therefore, this is not the ideal landmark for palpating the carotid pulse.

Suprasternal notch (Option C):

  • The suprasternal notch is the superior border of the manubrium of the sternum, at approximately T2-T3 vertebral level.
  • At this level, the common carotid arteries are still deep in the root of the neck, making the pulse difficult to palpate.
  • It is mainly used for landmarking the thoracic inlet and venous access (e.g., central line via subclavian or internal jugular approach).

Angle of mandible(Option D):

  • The angle of the mandible is located at the posteroinferior border of the mandible, roughly at C2 level.
  • The common carotid artery is medial and deep to the sternocleidomastoid, below the mandible, so palpation here is less reliable.
  • The external carotid artery or its branches may be closer superficially at this level, but the common carotid pulse is better felt lower, at the cricoid cartilage

question_text: A horizontal section of the neck is shown. The marked structure lies inside the carotid sheath, positioned between a large artery and a large vein, indicating its role as a major autonomic nerve. Identify the marked structure.
explanation:
Explanation:

The vagus nerve is located inside the carotid sheath, between:

  • Internal jugular vein laterally
  • Common/internal carotid artery medially
  • Carotid Sheath:
    • A tubular condensation of deep cervical fascia surrounding key structures in the neck:
      • Common carotid artery
      • Internal carotid artery
      • Internal jugular vein
      • Vagus nerve
    • The vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the internal jugular vein and the carotid arteries.
  • Anatomical Features:
    • The carotid sheath is wedged between the investing layer, pretracheal fascia, and prevertebral fascia, attached by loose areolar tissue.
    • Thickness:
      • Thicker around the common and internal carotid arteries.
      • Thinner over the internal jugular vein to allow for expansion during increased venous return.
    • Extent:
      • Extends from the base of the skull to the arch of the aorta.
    • Attachments:
      • Attached to the margins of the carotid canal and jugular fossa at the base of the skull.
      • Blends with the tunica adventitia at the arch of the aorta.
  • Relations:
    • The ansa cervicalis is embedded in the anterior wall of the sheath.
    • The cervical sympathetic chain is closely related to the posterior wall of the sheath, adhering to the prevertebral fascia.

Key Takeaway:

The vagus nerve, a critical component within the carotid sheath, plays an essential role in autonomic functions, underscoring the importance of understanding its anatomical relationships within the neck for both clinical and surgical contexts.

question_text: A patient has occasional blackouts and light-headedness. Studies reveal atherosclerotic plaques within the common carotid arteries and the bifurcation of the vessels. A carotid endartectomy is undertaken. Which nerve bundle running vertically within the carotid sheath must the surgeon be careful not to injure?
explanation:
In a carotid endarterectomy, surgeons enter the carotid artery and excise the diseased endothelium and media of the artery so that the lumen is left with a smooth lining. To do this, the surgeons must enter the carotid sheath, which means that any structure within that sheath or near that sheath might be injured. This question specifically asks which structure in the sheath could be injured, so the correct answer is the vagus nerve. The carotid sheath contains 2 nerves: the vagus and the superior ramus of ansa cervicalis. It also contains 3 vessels: internal carotid, common carotid, and internal jugular vein. Any of these structures could be damaged during the procedure.

The accessory nerve is most closely associated with the posterior triangle of the neck. It cuts through this triangle to innervate sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and lies posterior to the carotid vessels The cervical sympathetic trunk lies in front of the prevertebral muscles in the prevertebral fascia. The glossopharyngeal nerve comes out of the jugular foramen and divides into 2 branches- pharyngeal and lingual branches. This nerve sweeps near the carotid sheath, but it's not in the carotid sheath. The hypoglossal nerve travels lateral to the carotid vessels before entering the floor of the mouth. It crosses the carotid artery, but it's not in the sheath.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 900

question_text: Which of the following arteries does NOT supply the sternocleidomastoid muscle?

The sternocleidomastoid muscle has a dual head and a wide functional range in head and neck movement. Because of its anatomic course, it receives blood supply from several nearby arteries:

  • Occipital artery supplies the upper posterior region (Option A)
  • Posterior auricular artery gives branches near the mastoid attachment (Option B)
  • Suprascapular artery contributes via clavicular connections (Option D)

Clinical Importance:

Understanding these supplying arteries is crucial for safe surgical interventions in the carotid triangle and thyroid region to avoid compromising muscle function.

Key Takeaway:

The sternocleidomastoid muscle is primarily supplied by branches from the occipital, posterior auricular, and suprascapular arteries, with the superior thyroid artery being the exception that does not provide blood supply. This understanding is critical for surgical and anatomical applications in the neck region.

explanation:
Explanation:

The scalenus anterior lies anterior to the brachial plexus and is positioned in the anterior triangle of the neck, not forming the floor of the posterior triangle.

Posterior Triangle Boundaries:

  • Anterior: Posterior border of sternocleidomastoid muscle.
  • Posterior: Anterior border of trapezius muscle.
  • Inferior (Base): Superior aspect of the middle third of the clavicle.
  • Superior (Apex): Meeting point of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius at the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.

The floor of the posterior triangle is muscular, formed by:

  • Semispinalis Capitis (Option A)
  • Splenius Capitis (Option B)
  • Levator Scapulae (Option C)
  • Scalenus Medius
  • First Digitation of Serratus Anterior (rarely)
  • Roof:
    • Formed by theinvesting layer of the deep cervical fascia.
    • Contains platysma, external jugular vein, posterior jugular veins, and cutaneous nerves.
  • Subdivisions:
    • Divided into occipital triangle (upper part) andsupraclavicular triangle (lower part) by the inferior belly of the omohyoid muscle.

Key Takeaway:

In the posterior triangle of the neck[1], the floor is formed by muscles such as the semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis, and levator scapulae, while the scalenus anterior does not contribute to the floor structure, highlighting its unique role in the region's anatomy. Understanding these anatomical details is essential for clinical practice and surgical interventions in the neck.

question_text: An 60-year-old man comes to the clinic due for a follow-up after hospitalization. He was hospitalized two weeks ago for pneumonia and was treated with ampicillin-sulbactam. explanation:
Zenker's diverticulum, also known as pharyngoesophageal diverticulum, is a pharyngeal pouch that forms where the lower part of the throat and the upper part of the esophagus meet.

It is most common in older adults. If left untreated, it can negatively affect quality of life and can put a person at increased risk of aspiration and choking.

Zenker's diverticulum develops when the muscle between the throat and esophagus, known as the cricopharyngeus muscle, over-tightens, causing the throat above it to pouch out. Overtime, the pouch can enlarge as the muscles below it tighten excessively. Food can catch in this pouch or it can cause an obstruction. It can also make it difficult to take medications - particularly pills, which could get caught.

A person with Zenker's diverticulum may experience:

  • Difficulty swallowing
  • Bad breath
  • Chronic cough
  • A feeling of excessive phlegm or mucus in the throat
  • Sensation of "a lump in the throat"
  • Regurgitation of food (often hours after a meal)
  • Weight loss because eating is difficult

question_text: Which of the following statement is false regarding palsy showing in image ?

option_d: The nerve to inferior oblique carries parasympathetic fibers to the Otic ganglion
explanation:
The nerve to inferior oblique carries parasympathetic fibers to the ciliary ganglion and not from Otic ganglion.

There are two structures in the eye that receive parasympathetic innervation from the oculomotor nerve:

  • Sphincter pupillae- constricts the pupil, reducing the amount of light entering the eye.
  • Ciliary muscles- contracts, causes the lens to become more spherical, and thus more adapted to short range vision.

The pre-ganglionic parasympathetic fibres travel in the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve. Within the orbit, they branch off and synapse in the ciliary ganglion. The post-ganglionic fibres are carried to the eye via the short ciliary nerves.

Course of the oculomotor nerve:

  • The nerve lies on the anterior surface of the midbrain in between the posterior cerebral artery and the superior cerebellar artery in the interpeduncular fossa.
  • It then passes to the middle cranial fossa along the lateral dural wall of the cavernous sinus and divides into superior and inferior in its anterior part.
  • It enters the superior orbital fissure through the common tendinous ring.

question_text: A 47 year old male patient presented to his general practitioner with the classic triad of chemosis, pulsatile exophthalmos, and ocular bruit. He caught into road accident 2 weeks back and was admitted into hospital with severe head injuries. What could be the possible diagnosis associated with the given findings?
explanation:
Carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF) is an abnormal connection between the carotid artery and/or its branches and a large vein called the cavernous sinus. The cavernous sinus is located behind the eye and receives blood from brain, orbit, and pituitary gland. A carotid-cavernous fistula may be either direct (high-flow) or spontaneous (indirect/low flow)

CCF can develop either because of trauma or spontaneous causes. Traumatic CCF may occur after head injuries in which the intracavernous carotid artery is torn. Head injuries can range from minor falls to severe penetrating wounds. Traumatic CCF may also result from endovascular therapy. Spontaneous CCF usually results from a ruptured cavernous carotid aneurysm; however these fistulas may be congenital arteriovenous connections that open spontaneously in the setting of collagen vascular disease, atherosclerotic disease, hypertension, or childbirth.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is an uncommon benign tumor that originates in the lateral wall close to the sphenopalatine foramen. This tumor predominantly affects adolescent males and is locally aggressive, often invading the surrounding structures and tissues. JNA commonly presents with painless, progressive unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and rhinorrhea. JNA has a rich vascular supply primarily from the sphenopalatine artery. Macroscopically the tumor appears as a rounded circumscribed non-encapsulated mucosa covered mass. Microscopically the tumor shows haphazardly arranged collagen with an irregular vascular pattern. Because of the rich vascular supply, the embolization of the sphenopalatine artery and surgical resection of the tumor provides a good prognosis if JNA is diagnosed early enough.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with left eye vision loss and headache. She was in her usual state of health until 3 hours prior to presentation, when she developed vision loss and eye pain that worsened with eye movement. She reports that approximately 8 months ago she had left arm numbness that self resolved. On physical exam, her visual acuity is 20/185, and a sluggish response to light on the left eye with the swinging flash-light test is noted. The marked nerve is involved in this case. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Optic neuritis occurs when swelling (inflammation) damages the optic nerve - a bundle of nerve fibers that transmits visual information from your eye to your brain. Common symptoms of optic neuritis include pain with eye movement and temporary vision loss in one eye.

The swinging flashlight test can rule out intracranial damage to the optic nerve and the brain. To perform this test, shine a penlight into one eye to attain maximum pupil constriction, then quickly switch the light source to the other eye and back again.

question_text: A surgeon is performing a neck dissection and encounters the infrahyoid (strap) muscles. These muscles primarily receive innervation from a nerve loop in the cervical plexus known as the ansa cervicalis. However, one infrahyoid muscle has a different motor nerve supply. Which of the following infrahyoid muscles is NOT innervated by the ansa cervicalis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The thyrohyoid muscle is innervated by fibers from the hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII), specifically C1 fibers hitchhiking along its path. These C1 fibers do not join the ansa cervicalis loop, making the thyrohyoid uniquely innervated among the infrahyoid muscles.
Infrahyoid muscles stabilize or depress the hyoid bone during swallowing and phonation.
They include:

  • Sternohyoid (Option D)
  • Omohyoid (Option A)
  • Sternothyroid (Option C)
  • Thyrohyoid

Innervation details:

  • Ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) supplies sternohyoid, omohyoid, and sternothyroid
  • C1 via hypoglossal nerve supplies thyrohyoid (and geniohyoid)

Clinical relevance:
Damage to the hypoglossal nerve can affect thyrohyoid function, influencing laryngeal elevation and swallowing biomechanics.

Key Takeaway:

The thyrohyoid muscle is unique among infrahyoid muscles as it receives its innervation from a different source (C1 via hypoglossal nerve), unlike the others.

The ansa cervicalis innervates most infrahyoid muscles (omohyoid, sternothyroid, sternohyoid), while the thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by the nerve to thyrohyoid (C1) from the hypoglossal nerve, distinguishing it from the rest.

question_text: Twenty-four hours following a partial thyroidectomy where the inferior thyroid artery was also ligated (tied off), the patient now spoke with a hoarse voice (whisper), and had difficulty in breathing. Which nerve was injured?
explanation:
The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs with the inferior thyroid artery toward the lower lobes of the thyroid. This means that the recurrent laryngeal nerve would be at risk in any surgery involving the inferior thyroid artery or the inferior poles of the thyroid. The recurrent laryngeal nerve becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve at the inferior border of cricoid cartilage, and this nerve continues on to innervate all the muscles of the larynx with the exception of cricothyroid. So, an injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve might lead to hoarseness and difficulty breathing (due to a laryngeal spasm).

The internal branch of superior laryngeal runs with the superior laryngeal artery and pierces the thyrohyoid membrane. Ansa cervicalis is a branch of the cervical plexus which hangs in front of the internal jugular vein. It innervates the strap muscles, not the laryngeal muscles. Ansa subclavia is part of the sympathetic trunk which loops around the subclavian artery. Finally, the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery. This is the artery and nerve that might be damaged when removing the superior lobe of the thyroid.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 900

question_text: In performing a thyroidectomy, caution should be exercised when ligating (tying) the inferior thyroid artery, as it lies in a very close relationship to which nerve?
explanation:
The recurrent laryngeal nerve crosses the inferior thyroid artery near the lower lobe of the thyroid. This means that the recurrent laryngeal nerve would be at risk in any surgery involving the inferior thyroid artery or the inferior poles of the thyroid. The recurrent laryngeal nerve becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve at the inferior border of cricopharyngeus, and this nerve continues on to innervate all the muscles of the larynx with the exception of cricothyroid. So, you really need to take care to protect the recurrent laryngeal nerve injuring this structure could lead to hoarseness, permanent loss of voice, or even death due to a laryngeal spasm.

None of the other listed nerves are related to the inferior thyroid artery. Ansa cervicalis is a branch of the cervical plexus which hangs in front of the internal jugular vein. It innervates the strap muscles. The hypoglossal nerve winds behind the internal jugular vein, then sweeps around lateral to the carotid vessels and into the floor of the mouth, where it innervates the tongue muscles. The phrenic nerve lies on top of the anterior scalene muscles, it then travels through the thorax to innervate the diaphragm. Finally, the vagus is found in the carotid sheath, it is associated with the common carotid and the internal carotid arteries.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 900

question_text: Any manipulation of the superior thyroid artery must be undertaken with care not to damage its small companion nerve, the:

The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery, this artery and nerve might be damaged when removing the superior pole of the thyroid. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior laryngeal artery and provides sensory innervation to the mucous membrane of the larynx, superior to the vocal fold. The recurrent laryngeal nerve crosses the inferior thyroid artery, near the lower pole of the thyroid. This means that the recurrent laryngeal nerve would be at risk in any surgery involving the inferior thyroid artery or the inferior poles of the thyroid. The recurrent laryngeal innervates all the muscles of the larynx with the exception of cricothyroid. So, an injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve might lead to hoarseness and dificulty breathing.

The cervical sympathetic trunk lies in front of the prevertebral muscles in the prevertebral fascia, it would not be near the structures involved with thyroid surgery. The inferior root of ansa cervicalis is a branch of the cervical plexus. It innervates the strap muscles. Ansa cervicalis hangs in a loop over the carotid vessels; it is not associated with the thyroid gland.

question_text: A 30-year-old cricket player presents with pain over the outer (lateral) side of his right elbow. He reports increasing discomfort when gripping and lifting objects. On examination, there is clear tenderness directly over the lateral epicondyle, and pain is reproduced when he performs wrist extension against resistance. There is no history of a fall or direct injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Tennis elbow is a common overuse injury involving the common extensor tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle, especially the extensor carpi radialis brevis. Patients typically describe:

  • Pain over the lateral aspect of the elbow
  • Discomfort when gripping, lifting, or turning objects
  • Pain on resisted wrist extension

Tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) results from repeated strain on wrist extensor muscles.

  • The tendon gradually becomes irritated and painful at its attachment on the lateral epicondyle.
  • Common clinical features include:
    • Localized tenderness over the lateral epicondyle
    • Pain on resisted wrist or finger extension
    • Reduced grip strength
    • Symptoms aggravated by sports, lifting, or repetitive hand use
  • Most patients improve with rest, physiotherapy, NSAIDs, and activity modification.

Student elbow (Option A): Refers to olecranon bursitis, with swelling over the back of the elbow, not lateral pain.

Golfer elbow (Option B): Medial epicondylitis affecting wrist flexors; pain is on the inner side of the elbow.

Nursemaid elbow (Option D): Radial head subluxation in young children; not seen in adults and does not present with lateral epicondyle tenderness.

question_text: Mark the false statement regarding Accessory phrenic nerve?
option_a: The accessory phrenic nerve most commonly arises from the ansa cervicalis or the subclavian nerve
option_b: The accessory phrenic nerve most commonly joins with the phrenic nerve within the thorax (two-thirds) with the other third being within the neck at various locations.

explanation:
The accessory phrenic nerve is an anatomical variant seen in a little over one third of patients (36%). It most commonly arises from the ansa cervicalis, or slightly less commonly, the subclavian nerve. It is unknown as to how much the accessory phrenic nerve contributes to diaphragmatic function in these individuals.

Origin

The accessory phrenic nerve most commonly arises from the ansa cervicalis (45%) or the subclavian nerve (43%).

Rarely, it has also been seen to arise from the C3, C4 or C5 nerve roots, supraclavicular nerve, spinal accessory nerve, nerve to sternohyoid muscle or hypoglossal nerve.

Course

The accessory phrenic nerve most commonly joins with the phrenic nerve within the thorax (two-thirds) with the other third being within the neck at various locations.

question_text: A cervical plexus block is performed to provide anesthesia to the skin over the anterolateral neck region. This block usually targets the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerging at the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which of the following nerves would NOT be blocked during a standard cervical plexus block?
explanation:
Explanation:

The posterior auricular nerve is a branch of the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), not a branch of the cervical plexus. Therefore, it is not affected by a cervical plexus block that targets spinal nerve roots C2 to C4.
Cervical plexus cutaneous branches (C2 to C4):

  • Lesser occipital nerve (C2): Skin of posterolateral scalp (Option B)
  • Greater auricular nerve (C2 to C3): Skin over parotid region and angle of mandible (Option A)
  • Transverse cervical nerve (C2 to C3): Anterior neck skin
  • Supraclavicular nerves (C3 to C4): Skin over clavicle and upper chest (Option D)

Clinical relevance:
A superficial cervical plexus block is commonly used in surgeries involving the neck, clavicle, or ear region while preserving motor function of deeper neck muscles.

Key Takeaway:

In the case of a cervical block, all cutaneous nerves from the cervical plexus (such as the greater auricular, lesser occipital, and supraclavicular nerves) are blocked except for the posterior auricular nerve, which is derived from the facial nerve and remains unaffected. Understanding this distinction is crucial for anaesthetic procedures in the cervical region.

question_text: Which of the following are NOT a branch of external carotid artery in Kiesselbach's plexus?
option_d: Septal branch of superior labial artery
explanation:
Anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of ophthalmic artery (which itself is a branch of internal carotid artery).

Little's area is a highly vascular area located in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule.

Four (or five) arteries anastomose here to form a vascular plexus called Kiesselbach's plexus. Septal branch of the anterior ethmoidal artery (a branch of ophthalmic artery), Septal branch of the sphenopalatine artery (a branch of maxillary artery), septal branch of the greater palatine artery (a branch of maxillary artery) and septal branch of the superior labial artery (a branch of facial artery).

Occasionally septal branch of the posterior ethmoidal artery (a branch of ophthalmic artery) may also contribute to the plexus.

question_text: Which of the following is true about the nerve supply of the digastric muscle?

explanation:
Explanation:

  • Digastric Muscle:
    • Comprises two bellies (anterior and posterior) united by an intermediate tendon.
    • Origin:
      • Posterior Belly: Arises from the mastoid notch of the temporal bone.
      • Anterior Belly: Arises from the digastric fossa of the mandible.
  • Insertion:
    • Both belly's insert into the intermediate tendon, which is anchored to the hyoid bone.
  • Nerve Supply:
    • Posterior Belly: Supplied by the facial nerve (Option A).
    • Anterior Belly: Supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve from the mandibular nerve.

Key Takeaway:

The anterior belly of the digastric muscle is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, while the posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve.This reflects the developmental origin of each muscle belly from different pharyngeal arches.

question_text: Which nerve passes through the marked foramen ?
explanation:
The inferior alveolar nerve is a mandibular nerve branch. The inferior alveolar nerve is responsible for sensory innervation to the gingivae on the lower jaw. The inferior alveolar nerve also branches into the mylohyoid nerve and the mental nerve. As the inferior alveolar nerve descends the mandible, it will branch into the mylohyoid nerve to provide motor innervation to the mylohyoid muscle and the anterior belly of the digastric muscle.

The inferior alveolar nerve will then travel in the mandibular foramen until it reaches the mental foramen. Once at the mental foramen, the inferior alveolar nerve exits and becomes the mental nerve. The mental nerve is responsible for innervating the chin, lower lip, and gingivae.

The genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue. It is a large, thick muscle, which contributes significantly to the shape of the tongue.

question_text: A 65-year-old diabetic man presents with gradually worsening pain in his right shoulder. He also reports increasing stiffness and noticeable restrictions in all shoulder movements. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The combination of progressive shoulder pain, stiffness, and global limitation of movement is classic for frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis).
  • Diabetes is an important predisposing factor.
  • Unlike tendinitis or bursitis, where certain movements are more painful than others, frozen shoulder shows a uniform restriction of all movements.

Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) is a chronic inflammatory condition of the shoulder joint capsule.

Key features:

  • Gradual onset of pain
  • Increasing stiffness
  • Marked limitation of both active and passive movements
  • Often associated with diabetes, thyroid disorders, or prolonged immobilization
  • Surrounding muscles may show disuse atrophy due to chronic restriction

Pathology:

  • Shrinkage and thickening of the joint capsule
  • Fibroelastic proliferation
  • Adhesion formation within the capsule
  • Leads to pain and "frozen" mobility

The condition is self-limiting but may require several months to years for recovery. Physiotherapy, stretching, and pain control play major roles in management.

Subacromial bursitis (Option A): Painful arc of abduction; movement is painful but not uniformly restricted.

Supraspinatus tendinitis (Option B): Pain during abduction, especially between 60-120 degrees; range of motion is not globally reduced.

Fracture surgical neck humerus (Option C): Presents with acute trauma, bruising, severe pain, and inability to move immediately; not a gradual progressive stiffness.

question_text: Which compartment of TMJ (Temporomandibular joint) allows following movements?
explanation:
The given image shows Rotational movement and the inferior compartment allows rotational movements.

The superior compartment allows translational movements to occur at the joint. Translation (sliding) can be described as a movement in which every point of the moving object simultaneously has the same direction and velocity. An example of translation at the TMJ occurs when the mandible moves forward causing the teeth, condyles, and rami to all move in the same direction and to the same degree. This movement occurs between the superior surface of the articular disc and the inferior surface of the articular fossa. These movements include the:

  • Protrusion- the anterior movement of the mandible.
  • Retraction- the posterior movement of the mandible.
  • Left and right lateral deviation of the mandible - this usually refers to the acts of grinding and chewing.

The inferior compartment allows rotational movements. More specifically, rotation occurs between the superior surface of the condyle and the inferior surface of the articular disc. Rotational movement of the mandible can occur in all three planes: horizontal, frontal (vertical), and sagittal. These movements include the:

  • Depression- a movement of opening the mouth. This movement is mostly caused by gravity, however, if there is resistance, then muscles facilitate this movement.
  • Elevation- a strong movement of closing the mouth.

In most cases, both rotation and translation occur simultaneously. This results in complex movements that allow people to chew and talk.

question_text: In an auto accident, the patient's knee strikes the dashboard which in turn pushes the head of the femur posteriorly out of its socket. Which ligament is most likely ruptured by this posterior dislocation?
explanation:
Three ligaments comprise the hip joint capsule: pubofemoral, iliofemoral, and ichiofemoral. The iliofemoral ligament forms the anterior wall of the hip capsule, the pubofemoral lies beneath the joint, and the ischiofemoral ligament forms the posterior free margin of the hip capsule. Since the ischiofemoral ligament is the posterior edge of the hip capsule, it is the ligament that is most likely to be injured if the femur is dislocated posteriorly. The transverse acetabular ligament is a structure that bridges the acetabular notch and forms a bridge over the artery in the ligament of the femoral head.

The fibrous capsule around the hip joint does not attach to the posterior aspect of the femur. This means the femur can dislocate backwards. The hip joint is also less stable and more prone to dislocating when it is flexed (like when a person is sitting). So, posterior femoral dislocations are classically seen in car accidents, when a seated passenger bangs his or her knees into the dashboard and femur is pushed posteriorly.

question_text: In which of the following nerve injury eversion flick, high stepping gait is seen?
explanation:
Footdrop is another characteristic gait, which is caused by damage to the common or deep fibular nerve. The common fibular nerve wraps around the head of fibula, so blunt trauma or fracture here can lead to foot drop.

The deep fibular nerve innervates the muscles in the anterior compartment of the leg. These muscles dorsiflex the foot, which is required during the swing phase to clear the toes away from the ground.

If the deep fibular nerve is damaged, then the foot cannot be dorsiflexed, and drags along the ground during the swing phase. To compensate for the lack of dorsiflexion during the swing phase, the patient may evert the foot in a sudden motion, called an 'eversion flick'.

Another common compensatory movement is hyperflexion of the thigh at the hip to help the dropped foot clear the floor, known as "high steppage gait".

question_text: Circumvallate papillae of tongue derived from?

Explanation:

  • The circumvallate papillae (also called vallate papillae) are large, dome-shaped papillae located in front of the sulcus terminalis on the posterior part of the tongue.

Development of the Tongue

Formation of Anterior Two-Thirds (Option A&B):

Formation of Posterior One-Third:

  • The posterior one-third, including the circumvallate papillae, develops from the cranial part of the hypobranchial eminence.
  • A V-shaped groove (the sulcus terminalis) indicates the fusion line between the anterior and posterior parts.
  • The posterior most part of the tongue and the epiglottis arise from the caudal part of the hypobranchial eminence.

Key takeaways:

The tongue develops from lateral swellings merging to form the anterior two-thirds, with the posterior part arising from the hypobranchial eminence, marked by the sulcus terminalis, and innervated by different cranial nerves based on pharyngeal arch origins.

A defect in the hypobranchial eminence primarily affects the development of the epiglottis, while other laryngeal cartilages (arytenoid, corniculate, cuneiform) are unaffected because they develop from the pharyngeal arches.

question_text: Which structure contains postganglionic sympathetic fibers?
explanation:
When a nerve fiber reaches the sympathetic chain, there are three things that can happen. First, the nerve fibers can enter a ganglia, synapse at that level, and rejoin the spinal nerve via the grey ramus communicans. Second, the preganglionic nerve fibers can travel up or down the trunk, synapse in a ganglia at another level, and then rejoin a spinal nerve. This is how sympathetic fibers join spinal nerves at the cervical and lumbar levels, which are above and below the lateral horn. Third, some preganglionic fibers do not synapse in the trunk and, instead, form splanchnic nerves. These nerves descend into the abdomen and synapse in other ganglia.

The greater thoracic splanchnic nerve contains preganglionic fibers that are destined to synapse in the celiac plexus. The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides motor and sensory innervation to the upper esophagus and pharynx. Finally, the vagus nerve is a mixed nerve that carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers. None of these nerves carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers.

The ulnar nerve innervates muscles of the hand, arm, and provides some sensory innervation to skin of the hand and arm. It is derived from ventral rami of spinal nerves, all of which carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers (for vascular smooth muscle, arrector pili muscles, and sweat glands).

question_text: Identify the marked structure

Explanation:

The pyriform sinus (also called piriform recess or piriform fossa) is a mucosal recess located on either side of the laryngeal inlet in the hypopharynx (the lower part of the pharynx).

Anatomical Location:

  • Lies between:
    • Medially: the laryngeal inlet (opening of the larynx)
    • Laterally: the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane
  • It's part of the laryngopharynx, which is posterior to the larynx.

Function:

  • Guides food and liquid around the laryngeal inlet into the oesophagus during swallowing
  • Helps prevent aspiration by channelling material away from the airway

Clinical Relevance:

1. Foreign Body Entrapment:

  • Fish bones, pills, or small objects often lodge here
  • Easily visualised with flexible laryngoscopy or imaging

2. Internal Branch of Superior Laryngeal Nerve:

  • This nerve lies beneath the mucosa of the pyriform sinus
  • Vulnerable to injury during surgery or foreign body removal
  • Damage can lead to loss of sensation above the vocal cords → increased aspiration risk

3. Pyriform Sinus Fistula:

  • A congenital anomaly (from remnants of the 3rd or 4th pharyngeal pouch)
  • It can cause recurrent neck infections in children.

4. Visualization:

  • Seen during laryngoscopy, endoscopy, or barium swallow studies
  • Appears as a pear-shaped depression on either side of the laryngeal inlet

Thyroid cartilage(Option A): The thyroid cartilage is the largest of the laryngeal cartilages. It forms the bulk of the anterior wall of the larynx and gives rise to the visible laryngeal prominence (commonly known as the Adam’s apple).

  • Lies at the level of the C4-C5 vertebrae
  • Situated anterior to the larynx, superior to the cricoid cartilage

Epiglottis(Option B): The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage that sits at the top of the larynx. Its main role is to protect the airway during swallowing by covering the laryngeal inlet.

Vallecula(Option D): The term vallecula (plural: valleculae) refers to an anatomical depression or groove. It's used in several contexts in the body, but most commonly:

  • Oropharyngeal vallecula: Can collect food or secretions; sometimes examined in swallowing studies.
  • Cerebellar vallecula: Important in brain imaging and neurosurgery as a landmark.

question_text: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the trachea through its terminal branches. Injury to this nerve would most likely affect which of the following functions?
option_a: Secretomotor to glands in the mucosa
explanation:
Explanation:

The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides motor innervation to the trachealis muscle, the smooth muscle that helps regulate tracheal diameter. Injury to the nerve would impair this motor function.

Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Functions:

  • Motor: Supplies the trachealis muscle.
  • Sensory: Supplies mucosa below the vocal cords, including most of the tracheal mucosa.
  • Secretomotor: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers come from the vagus nerve.
  • Vasomotor: Sympathetic fibers control the vasomotor tone. (Option B)

Thus, motor supply to the trachealis is the single most specific function lost with recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.

Secretomotor to glands in the mucosa (Option A): Secretomotor fibers arise from the vagus nerve's parasympathetic components, not specifically from the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Sensory to the mucous membrane (Option C): The recurrent laryngeal nerve does provide sensory fibers below the vocal cords, but this is not the most specific or primary feature tested compared to its motor role.

question_text: The nerve that innervates all the muscle of larynx except cricothyroid muscle-
explanation:
The inferior laryngeal nerve is the continuation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, superior to the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage. It innervates the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle, which is responsible for abducting the vocal folds. The inferior laryngeal nerve also innervates all of the other intrinsic muscles of the larynx, with the exception of the cricothyroid muscle. The pharyngeal branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the pharynx, but not to the larynx. The glossopharyngeal nerve only provides motor innervation to stylopharyngeus. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle, which is responsible for stretching the vocal ligaments. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is responsible for providing sensory innervation to the mucosa of the larynx, superior to the true vocal fold. The thyrohyoid nerve is a branch of ansa cervicalis, it innervates the thyrohyoid muscle, which elevates the larynx and depresses the hyoid bone (or helps to fix the hyoid in space, so that other muscles, such as tongue muscles, can work).

question_text: Which of the following muscles is an abductor of the vocal cord?

question_text: Following thyroid surgery, it was noted that a patient frequently aspirated fluid into her lungs. Upon examination it was determined that the area of the piriform recess above the vocal fold of the larynx was numb. What nerve may have been injured?
option_a: External branch of the superior laryngeal
option_c: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal
explanation:
The internal branch of the superior laryngeal is a sensory nerve that pierces the thyrohyoid membrane along with the superior laryngeal artery. It supplies sensory fibers to the mucous membrane of the larynx, superior to the vocal folds. Since this area lost sensation, it appears that the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve must have been injured. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is a motor nerve that innervates the cricothyroid muscle, it does not provide any sensory innervation to the larynx. The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends from the thorax and provides motor innervation to the upper esophagus, lower pharynx, and all the laryngeal muscles except cricothyroideus.

The hypoglossal nerve supplies motor innervation to the muscles of the tongue. The lingual nerve is a sensory nerve for the anterior 2/3 of the tongue. These nerves are not important for innervating the larynx.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 1066

question_text: The laryngeal muscle most responsible for stretching (elongating) the vocal ligament is the-
explanation:
Cricothyroid draws the thyroid cartilage forward, tensing the vocal ligaments. This is the one muscle innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. Posterior cricoarytenoid is a very important muscle; it's the only muscle that abducts the vocal folds. This muscle is innervated by the inferior laryngeal nerve, which is a continuation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. If this muscle is denervated, the vocal folds may be paralyzed in an adducted position, which would prevent air from entering the trachea. Lateral cricoarytenoid, thyroarytenoid, and arytenoid are all muscles that adduct the vocal folds. They are all innervated by the inferior laryngeal nerve.

Reference: Textbook of B. D. Chaurasia: Human Anatomy, Volume 3, 8th Edition, Page Number-1066.

question_text: Identify the muscle most responsible for the abduction of the vocal folds is the :
explanation:
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts the vocal folds. This muscle is innervated by the inferior laryngeal nerve, which is a continuation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve. If this muscle is denervated, the vocal folds may be paralyzed in an adducted position, which would prevent air from entering the trachea. Arytenoid, lateral cricoarytenoid, and thyroarytenoid all adduct the vocal folds. Cricothyroid is the only laryngeal muscle innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal. It tenses the vocal ligaments by tipping the thyroid cartilage forward relative to the cricoid cartilage.

Reference: Textbook of Gray's Anatomy for students, 3rd Edition, Head and neck, Page number - 1053

question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with a fish bone lodged in the pyriform sinus. During endoscopic removal, there is accidental nerve injury. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be damaged in this situation?
option_c: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
option_d: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (from vagus, CN X) pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and provides sensory innervation to the mucosa of the larynx above the vocal cords and the pyriform sinus.
  • Because this nerve runs just beneath the mucosa of the pyriform fossa, it is highly vulnerable to injury during the removal of foreign bodies like fish bones.
  • Injury results in loss of sensation in the supraglottic larynx and pyriform sinus, increasing the risk of aspiration.
  • Hence, the most likely nerve injured in this case is the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.

Explanation of other options:

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option A): Supplies motor innervation to intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid) and sensory below the vocal cords, not at the pyriform sinus.

Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option B): Provides sensation to the oropharynx and the posterior one-third of the tongue, not the pyriform sinus.

External branch of superior laryngeal nerve (Option D): Supplies the cricothyroid muscle (motor), not sensory to the pyriform sinus.

question_text: A 50-year-old male presents with hoarseness of voice. His cough reflex is intact. Laryngoscopy shows both vocal cords fixed in the cadaveric position. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
option_a: Bilateral external and internal laryngeal nerve
option_b: Bilateral internal and recurrent laryngeal nerve
option_d: Bilateral recurrent and external laryngeal nerve
explanation:
Explanation:

The cadaveric position of the vocal cords occurs when all intrinsic muscles of the larynx are paralyzed, including both abductors and adductors. This happens when there is bilateral damage to both the recurrent laryngeal nerves and the external laryngeal nerves.

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerves supply all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid.
  • External laryngeal nerves supply the cricothyroid muscle, the only tensor of the vocal cords.
  • Loss of both results in complete paralysis, placing the cords in the cadaveric position. (Option C)

Nerve Functions:

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Motor to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.
  • External laryngeal nerve: Motor to cricothyroid (important for tension and pitch).
  • Internal laryngeal nerve: Sensory above the vocal cords and responsible for cough reflex. (Options A & B)

Clinical Correlation:

  • Cough reflex intact means the internal laryngeal nerve is functional, helping rule out options containing internal nerve injury.
  • Cadaveric position indicates complete bilateral motor paralysis, requiring combined recurrent + external laryngeal nerve involvement.

question_text: The nerve supply of the larynx above the level of the vocal cords is by -
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The superior laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus, is responsible for sensation above the vocal cords.
  • It divides into two branches:
    • Internal branch → pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and provides sensory innervation to the mucosa of the larynx and hypopharynx above the vocal cords.
    • External branch → motor supply to the cricothyroid muscle.
  • Overall innervation of the larynx:
    • Motor fibres:
      • Recurrent laryngeal nerve → all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid.
      • External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve → cricothyroid muscle.
    • Sensory fibers:
      • Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve → mucosa above the vocal cords.
      • Recurrent laryngeal nerve → mucosa below the vocal cords.
      • Recurrent laryngeal nerve course:

On the right side, it loops around the subclavian artery before ascending in the tracheoesophageal groove.

On the left side, it hooks around the arch of the aorta and then ascends, making it longer and more vulnerable to injury than the right.

Superior laryngeal nerve anatomy:

  • Originates from the inferior ganglion of the vagus.
  • Runs posterior to the internal carotid artery.
  • Divided into internal and external branches near the greater horn of the hyoid bone.

Explanation of incorrect options:

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Option B): supplies sensory innervation below the vocal cords and motor fibers to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid.

Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C): carries taste and general sensation from the posterior one-third of the tongue and sensation from the oropharynx; it does not supply the larynx.

External laryngeal nerve (Option D): a motor branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that acts only on the cricothyroid muscle, not the mucosa above the vocal cords.

question_text: A trauma patient presents with upper airway obstruction. During emergency assessment, a clinician identifies the cricoid cartilage as a key landmark, located at the inferior border of the larynx. Several important structures and anatomical transitions occur at this level. Which of the following is NOT located at or associated with the level of the cricoid cartilage?
option_c: Common carotid artery can be compressed and palpated
option_d: Isthmus of the thyroid gland lies at this level
explanation:
Explanation:

The thyroid isthmus typically lies lower, spanning 2nd to 4th tracheal rings, which are located below the level of the cricoid cartilage. Therefore, the isthmus is not associated with the C6 level.

Cricoid cartilage corresponds to C6 vertebral level and serves as a major surgical and radiological landmark. Structures at C6 level:

  • End of larynx and beginning of trachea (Option A)
  • End of pharynx and beginning of esophagus(Option B)
  • Cricopharyngeus muscle forms upper esophageal sphincter
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve enters larynx
  • Vertebral artery enters transverse foramen of C6
  • Clinical relevance:
  • Sellick maneuver (cricoid pressure) applied during intubation
  • Airway obstruction assessment and cricothyrotomy location reference

Key Takeaway:

The cricoid cartilage is crucial for understanding neck anatomy, marking the junction of the larynx and trachea, the pharynx and esophagus, and allowing for carotid artery palpation. However, the isthmus of the thyroid gland is positioned at the C7 vertebra, not at the level of the cricoid cartilage.

the posterior end of the inferior turbinate lies close to the opening of the Eustachian tube in the nasopharynx. explanation:
Vocalis represents the innermost fibers of the thyroarytenoid muscle, from the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage. Because vocalis inserts on the vocal ligament, it can relax very specific segments of the vocal ligament to adjust the pitch. Although there are many muscles that insert on the other pieces of cartilage listed, vocalis is the only one that can provide for such fine control of tone because it is inserting right on the vocal ligament.
